units: the writer answers a question his correspondent raised earlier
two string instruments are sitting in a place where instruments are made
on the first one, a finger pulls the string aside and releases it to start the sound
on the second, a bow drawn across the string produces the sound
the tone of the first dies away as soon as it appears
the tone of the second can be held for as long as the movement lasts
the first allows several strings to sound together
the second hardly manages more than two strings at a time
the writer recommends the first one for backing a singer
text: You asked me a while back to sort out the two string instruments sitting in the workshop, so here goes. On the first one, a finger pulls a string aside and lets it snap back, and that release starts the sound. On the second, you drag a bow across the string and the tone builds up under it. Everything else follows from the way the sound begins. Pluck a string and the note dies the moment it appears. Bow a string and you can stretch the note out as long as your arm keeps moving, swelling it or letting it fade whenever you choose. One more gap is worth knowing about. The plucked instrument takes several strings at once, so a whole chord sits under your hand, while the bowed one barely manages two together. Backing a singer, take the plucked one. Carrying a single line, take the other.

units: the text sorts noises into three categories
the first category covers sounds that never break off
the ear stops noticing those steady sounds
the second category gathers sounds that come back at intervals
the third category concerns very short and violent impacts
an impact of that kind can damage hearing in an instant
how long the exposure lasts weighs as much as how loud the sound is
three protections are named: move away, put up a barrier, shorten the exposure
hearing cells that have been destroyed never grow back
text: What exactly counts as noise? The answer sorts the phenomena into three families. The first covers steady sounds, the hum of a machine among them, which the ear stops registering after a while. The second gathers sounds that come back at intervals, an alarm chiming over and over, never letting you forget they are there. The third holds the short, violent impacts that can wreck hearing in a second. Should the racket of a building site worry anyone more than the murmur of a wide street? Specialists answer that how long you stay exposed weighs as much as how loud the source is. What protection works? Three measures come recommended: move away from the source, put an absorbing wall in between, cut the listening short. Does damaged hearing mend itself? Destroyed cells never grow back, and prevention remains the only route.

units: a learner recounts out loud a lesson he was given
the specialist asks him to listen in silence to a struck key
at first the learner hears only one sound
several strings in fact belong to a single key
the specialist deliberately slackens one of the strings
the learner then hears a regular throbbing
removing that throbbing is the point of the operation
the specialist plays a run of neighboring notes
the learner tightens the moving part too far during his own attempt
by the end, two strings no longer produce any throbbing
text: The student went back over his lesson out loud, step by step, in the order it had actually happened. The tuner had asked him first to say nothing and just listen while she struck a single key. He told her that all he could hear was a single note. She pushed back: three strings vibrate behind that key. Then she slackened one of them on purpose, and he said a slow throb had come up, like a wave rising and dropping away. Tuning, she explained, means getting rid of that throb. After that she played a whole scale so he could hear the neighboring notes. She handed him the wrench at last and let him turn the tension pin himself. He cranked it too far, the throb sped up, and she told him to work with a lighter hand. By the close of the session, two strings had fallen silent for each other.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: old rooms were low and hung with cloth
sound died away quickly in them
that quick fade allowed fast successions of notes
taller stone rooms were built afterwards
sound lingered there long after it was made
fast passages turned confused in those rooms
the writers of music then spaced their notes out and lengthened them
adding padded seats and an audience cut the lingering sound down
musical writing grew fast again after that
the text concludes that materials shaped music as much as taste did
text: Look at what happens to a piece of music when the room it is played in changes size and shape. Players once worked in low chambers hung with heavy cloth, where sound died almost as soon as it left the strings. With nothing left hanging in the air, they could run fast notes together and keep them clean. Then tall halls of bare stone went up, and every sound dragged a long tail behind it. The same quick passages turned to mush, so composers slowed their writing down, stretched the chords out, and traded quick ornament for long held tones. Later those halls filled with padded seats and packed listeners, and the echo shrank again. Writing picked up speed once more, and the pace tightened. Stone and fabric, in other words, shaped the scores as much as any taste of the people listening did.

units: students sitting at the back catch only part of the instructions
the cause lies with the surfaces of the room rather than with the speaker
bare walls throw back sounds that then mix together
everyone speaks louder, which raises the noise further
specialists call that mechanism a spiral
absorbing panels are put up on the ceiling
pads under the chairs do away with the scraping
the layout of the tables turns voices toward the listeners
teachers strain their voices less once those changes are made
the money spent stays modest
text: In plenty of classrooms, the students sitting at the back catch no more than half of what they are told. The trouble rarely starts with the teacher's voice. It starts with the surfaces of the room. A bare space throws sound back, the returns pile onto each other, and syllables blur. So everybody speaks up, and the level climbs higher still. Acousticians call that a noise spiral. Breaking out of it takes surprisingly little work. Porous panels go on the ceiling and soak up part of what bounces. Felt pads fixed under the chair legs kill off the scraping. Tables get turned so that mouths face ears. Where those steps have been taken, teachers push their voices far less than they used to. The outlay stays small, and you can hear the difference from the very first lesson onward.

units: a woman upstairs plays a plucked string instrument
a man on the ground floor plays a worn guitar
the narrator likens the two kinds of music to two kinds of rain
the music from upstairs makes separate notes parted by silences
the music from below forms a continuous fabric that cannot be counted
the power fails during a storm
the two neighbors then play at the same time without having agreed on it
the narrator listens from the stairwell of the building
the blend makes a music unlike either of the first two
the neighbors stop playing when the power returns
text: The woman who lives above me plays a harp, and the man on the ground floor works at a battered guitar. In the end I came to compare the two the way you might compare two kinds of rain. Hers falls in separate drops, each note clean, each one held apart from the next by a polite silence. His comes down as a sheet, strings answering strings, fingers scraping, nothing you could ever count. During a storm one evening the power failed across the building, and the two of them began playing at the same moment, with no word between them. From the stairwell I heard the drops land on the sheet. It was neither of their musics but a third one, which neither could have written down. When the lights came back they stopped, doors closed, and the building went back to being two apartments stacked up.

units: the preparation follows three ordered steps
the room holding the most furniture is the one to choose
any device making a background noise has to be switched off
a thick cloth is hung behind the person speaking
the microphone goes at chin height and slightly off to the side
the tilt keeps expelled air from striking the diaphragm
the stand belongs on the floor rather than on a piece of furniture
a short stretch of silence is recorded to gauge the room noise
monitoring is done on headphones and not through a speaker
one whole take is kept before any editing
text: Before recording a voice at home, get the room, the microphone, and the take ready, in that order. The room: pick whichever one holds the most furniture, shut the windows, switch off anything that blows or hums, and hang a thick blanket behind where you will stand. The microphone: bring it up to chin height, a hand's width from your mouth, tilted off to one side so the breath behind consonants never strikes the diaphragm. Set it on a weighted stand resting on the floor, never on the table, since wood carries every bump straight through. The take: record a short stretch of silence first, which gives you a measure of the room noise. Keep your volume even, without drifting closer or farther away. Monitor on headphones, never through a speaker. Save one whole spare take before you cut anything.

units: work on a concert venue has just been finished
complaints had piled up over a whole season
low sounds became inaudible from the far rows back
an acoustic study was commissioned and then handed to those in charge
the decision was made to open up the vaulted ceiling
the panels that threw the sound back were taken down
the armchairs were replaced by seats whose absorption never varies
the stage floor was given a slope
a musical ensemble played with no audience to test the venue
those in charge will wait a whole season before drawing conclusions
text: Renovation work at the concert venue wrapped up at the end of last week, at the end of an operation the musicians followed closely. It had begun after a full season of complaints: ever since the ceiling was redone, the low instruments vanished for anyone sitting in the far rows back. An acoustic study was commissioned and then handed to the management, which decided to open the vaulted ceiling back up. Crews took down the panels that threw the sound back, swapped the old armchairs for seats whose absorption never varies, and put a slope into the stage floor. An ensemble played behind closed doors to measure how the room now answers. Management has announced that performances will resume, warning at the same time that no final verdict will come before a whole season of use.

units: you hear the workshop before you catch sight of it
the craftsman strikes a heated piece of metal
each blow makes a short sound thrown back by the metal walls
the pitch of the sound shifts because the metal cools
the sound turns higher as the material stiffens
the sandy floor soaks up part of what bounces back
a blower keeps the fire going and makes a steady noise
the ear grows used to that steady noise and keeps only the blows
the silence after the stop seems sharper than it really is
text: You hear the forge well before you ever catch sight of it. The smith hammers away at a bar pulled hot from the fire, and each blow tears out a short, near-shrill sound that comes straight back off the sheet-metal walls. Because the bar cools under the hammer, the pitch shifts: it climbs as the metal stiffens, and it drops when the flame softens the bar again. Sand on the floor swallows part of what bounces, so the din stays bearable for whoever works there. At the far end of the shop, a blower breathes steadily on the coals, and its steady drone lies under everything else. The ear settles into that drone and ends up hearing only the blows. When the hammer stops, the silence seems deeper than it really is, because hearing holds on to the trace of the sound a moment longer.

units: the listener has no say in the music played in public places
that music is played to slow customers down
the writer locates the problem in the absence of any prior agreement
no way of stopping the music is offered
people who hear poorly are put out more than others
background music covers voices and makes conversation tiring
a first measure sets up stretches of time with nothing playing
those stretches would be posted at the door and would cost nothing
a second measure lowers the volume until talking becomes possible
a third measure hands the setting over to the staff of the place
text: Hardly anyone gets to pick the music they hear in public anymore. Walk into a store, an elevator, a waiting room, and a chorus greets you, tuned to slow your step along the shelves. The problem is not taste, it is consent. Nobody asked whether you wanted to listen, and nobody offers you a way to shut it off. For people who hear poorly it runs worse: the wash of sound covers voices and turns a conversation into hard work. So what could actually be done about it? First, make silence available. A stretch of the day with nothing playing, posted at the door, costs nothing at all. Second, drop the level until two customers can talk without raising their voices. Third, hand the dial to the staff, since they are the ones stuck with the loop from open to close. None of this calls for a law.
